tagline.text: Biliran's hidden island of green hills meeting a jade-blue sea

items.credit: Rodel Bontes / CC BY-SA 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: In the sea west of Biliran Island, beside Maripipi Island, four small islets are linked by a rock causeway. From the grass-covered hilltop viewpoint you can look down over a jade-blue sea and a volcanic island, and the clear waters of its marine protected area make for excellent snorkeling and diving — a hidden gem of the Visayas.
Sambawan Island belongs to Biliran, a small province attached to the north of Leyte, and administratively is a barangay of the volcanic island of Maripipi. It sits in the Samar Sea about

off the west coast of the Biliran mainland, and is less a single island than a row of four small islets. On the sheltered side of the largest islet is a beach of white sand mixed with pebbles, and at low tide, exposed rock causeways let you walk across to the neighboring islets.

The island's icon is the viewpoint atop the grassy hill behind the beach. Climb about 130 steps and the view opens up on every side: jade and deep-blue sea layered below, the cone-shaped volcanic island of Maripipi behind, and the mountains of the Biliran mainland in the distance. The scene of green hills meeting the sea that so often appears in Philippine travel photos was taken right here.

The waters around the island are managed as a marine protected area, so the coral is healthy and the water very clear. At the nearby Buga and Puntod reefs, lucky visitors have reported sightings of dolphins, manta rays, and sharks, and the spot has quietly built a reputation among divers. The island has only a single modest resort doubling as a dive camp and a campground, and electricity, from solar panels and a generator, is often available only in the evening.

Because the journey is inconvenient, few people make it here, and with no large resorts or restaurants, the island still feels like an uninhabited one. It suits travelers who want scenery and quiet over amenities, snorkeling and freediving enthusiasts, and anyone who wants to pitch a tent with friends and spend a night watching the stars.
Climb about 130 steps for a 360-degree view over the sea and Maripipi's volcanic island. The sea color is most vivid in the early morning and late afternoon, when the sun sits low.

blocks.title: Snorkeling in the marine protected area

children.text: Just a few steps out from the beach, you'll see coral and tropical fish. The water is clear with great visibility, and many people come to practice freediving.

You can dive the surrounding reefs through the island's dive camp or operators on the Biliran mainland. Sheer coral walls and large schools of fish are the highlights, and you should book gear and an instructor in advance.

blocks.title: Crossing the rock causeway at low tide

children.text: When the tide goes out, the rock causeways linking the islets are exposed, letting you walk to the next one. Check the high-tide time and wear aqua shoes when crossing.
Pitch a tent and stay the night, and you'll have the island to yourself once the day-trippers leave. With almost no light pollution, you can see the Milky Way on a clear night.
The island is small enough to watch both the sun rising in the east and setting over the sea to the west. Wait at the viewpoint and you'll catch the sky and sea coloring together.
On calm days, rent a kayak and paddle around the island to see its rocky cliffs and small beaches.

Ferries are infrequent, so if you miss the boat back, you'll need to stay overnight on Maripipi. It's best to confirm departure times the day before.
Biliran has no clearly defined dry season and sees rain year-round, but
March–June

, when the sea is calm and the sun plentiful, is the best time to visit Sambawan. Water clarity is excellent for snorkeling during this period, and the sea color from the viewpoint is at its most vivid. Daytime temperatures run around
, so the sun is very intense on the largely shadeless hill.
July–September
brings frequent showers from the southwest monsoon, and from
October to February

, typhoons and the northeast monsoon (Amihan) often raise waves in the Samar Sea high enough to keep boats docked. This area sits along a frequent typhoon path, so during the rainy season and winter months, it's important to check the weather forecast and coast guard departure restrictions before setting out, and to build buffer days into your schedule. Local campers crowd the island during Holy Week and summer-break weekends, so a weekday visit is recommended.

On the island, a single resort that doubles as a dive camp runs rooms and cottages, with fan rooms shared by several people running about

a night. Rooms are limited and fill up early on weekends and holidays, so book ahead. Bringing your own tent lets you stay cheaply in the designated camping area. Before or after visiting the island, it's convenient to stay in Naval, the capital of Biliran, where simple hotels and guesthouses around the port and market run about
a night.

It's best to plan as if there are no restaurants on the island. Some resorts can arrange meals if you ask in advance, but most visitors buy fish, meat, rice, fruit, and water at Naval's public market and grill them over charcoal on the island. Drinking water can also be bought by the gallon on the island, but it's safer to bring plenty. In the coastal towns of Biliran and Leyte, you can commonly find kinilaw, raw fish cured in vinegar, charcoal-grilled fish, and seafood simmered in coconut milk, and binagol, a Leyte sticky-rice specialty, is also available at Naval's market.
There are no ATMs on the island or on Maripipi. Bring plenty of cash from Naval or Tacloban to cover the boat fare, entrance fee, and accommodation.

Chartered boat fares are per boat, so the more people you have, the cheaper it gets per person. Finding travel companions through your Naval accommodation or the Biliran tourism community can cut the cost significantly.
It's best to bring your own snorkel gear, life vest, and aqua shoes. The island doesn't have many available to rent.
The viewpoint hill has almost no shade. Bring a hat and water, and avoid climbing at midday.
Electricity is often available only for a few hours in the evening, so a power bank and flashlight are essential.
Cell signal is weak, so be sure to firmly arrange your return time with the boat operator before heading out to the island.
To protect the coral reef, use reef-safe sunscreen and carry all your trash back out with you.
If you have time left after returning to Naval, a half-day tour of the waterfalls, hot springs, and rice terraces on the Biliran mainland is also worthwhile.

Waves in the Samar Sea rise sharply in the afternoon and during monsoon season. Boat departures are restricted in bad weather, so never push to set out, and check the latest notices from the Maripipi tourism office for entrance fees and stay regulations.
Always check that the boat has life vests on board, and avoid boats that carry more passengers than their capacity allows.
The rock causeway submerges and the current quickens at high tide. Check tide times before crossing, and allow plenty of time to return.
Standing on or touching coral, and collecting shells or fish, are prohibited within the marine protected area.
The island has no medical facilities, so an injury means taking a boat back to the mainland. Bring basic first-aid supplies and antiseptic.
The hill's steps and grass become slippery when it rains, and the risk of heatstroke is high at midday.
